synth.verdict:
WHAT IS ALREADY STRONG. The bones are good:
- A true arrival axis runs from the 6 ft front door pair (x 34.5-40.5) through 28'-6" of living room to the 16 ft glass wall (x 29.5-45.5) and the pond.
- Living and kitchen are one open 44'-0" x 28'-6" room (about 1,200 sf) with no wall between them.
- There is a real scullery, a sound-isolated office, and a primary suite that sits at the far end of the house with its own side porch.
- The roof is clean: one main 8:12 gable with hips on the wings.
None of this needs to move.

WHAT HOLDS IT BACK FROM FEELING HIGH-END:
(1) The primary closet is really a corridor. The dressing room is 20'-0" x 8'-0" (160 sf), but 37 sf of it is the walk-through strip at x 86-90.6. That leaves about 3'-7" of aisle between two 13'-7" wardrobe runs (about 27 LF of rod, drawn about 19" deep instead of 24"), with no island and one 3 ft window. Michael is right that it is tight.
(2) The primary bath has enough area (20'-0" x 10'-6", 210 sf), but it is a 10'-6" strip.
- The WC, a wedged drop-in tub (8'-2" slot) and a small shower (about 5'-7" x 4'-7" clear) all sit in one 5 ft band on the back wall.
- The three sinks are split unevenly, and they face the WC door 3'-7" away.
- The bath is reached through the closet.
The real cause is that bath, closet and bedroom are three full-width strips stacked front to back. More square footage alone does not fix that.
(3) The great room is wide but low.
- The ceilings are flat: 12 ft over the living room, 11 ft over the kitchen, with an accidental-looking 1 ft step at x 52. That is a height-to-width ratio of 0.42 over a 28'-6" span; grand rooms run 0.6-0.75.
- About 9 ft of volume (ridge about 21'-10") is hidden in attic directly above it.
- The arrival axis is blocked on foot by chairs, the coffee table and a 10'-6" sofa that has its back to the pond.
- The 16'-0" x 3'-6" courtyard notch at the kitchen front (52-68 x 59-62.5) breaks the front wall and leaves the sink window looking into a dark recess.
(4) Smaller luxury gaps:
- The garage entry door (x 87-90, y 40) looks straight into the primary bedroom door 8 ft away.
- There is no mudroom; the drop zone is an 18" bench in the hall.
- Guests reach the powder room through the office vestibule.
- Bedroom 2 (331 sf) is bigger than the primary bedroom but has a 27 sf closet.
- The halls get no daylight.

WHAT I WOULD NOT DO. A 14 ft great-room plate was checked and ruled out: the raised back slope would ride up to 2 ft above the garage's side-gable rake between y 40 and 48.7, creating new valleys against the bonus-room roof. A flipped primary suite (bedroom facing the pond) was also ruled out: it shrinks the bath, faces the party terrace from about 2 ft away, and runs into the berm.

The three moves that would make the biggest difference:
- Primary option B: push the bath back 7 ft and give the closet a real room.
- Great room option G2: a cathedral living room plus a plan re-set, with the notch filled.
- The mud-laundry garage entry.

No growth. Move the bedroom/closet wall from y 16 to y 17. Split the back 20'-0" x 19'-6" zone down the middle at x 96.

CLOSET, 86-96 x -2.5 to 17 (10'-0" x 19'-6", 195 sf; was 160):

- Window seat under a new 5'-0" back window.
- 3'-0" cased opening from the bedroom.
- Storage is about the same as today: 27 LF single-hang, about 40-45 LF with double-hang. The gain is the aisle, the light and a real room shape.

BATH, 96-106 x -2.5 to 17 (10'-0" x 19'-6", 195 sf; was 210), entered from the closet by a hinged 2'-10" door at x 96:
- WC room 4'-6" x 5'-6" with a hinged 2'-4" door and a high window.
- Shower 5'-6" x 6'-6" (was about 5'-7" x 4'-7" clear) with a bench, keeping the tempered window at x 106.
- Facing 6'-0" vanities about 5'-11" apart: his on x 96, hers on x 106.
- A 5'-0" freestanding tub with 6" clear all round, under a tempered, obscured side window.

BEDROOM: 86-106 x 17-32, 20'-0" x 15'-0" (300 sf; was 320). The bed re-centers at x 99.
options.roof_impact: None. The same 'Primary bath' and 'Office and primary' hips. Window changes only: the old 6 ft back tub window becomes a 5 ft closet window plus a 2'-6" high WC window, and the x 106 bath window moves to y 11.5-15.5.
options.tradeoffs:
Cheapest fix and no roof work. But:
- The bath is still reached through the closet, so the closet needs humidity control and exhaust.
- The WC is near the code minimum (about 4'-2" clear wide, about 3'-2" in front of the bowl).
- The tub looks at the side porch, not the pond.
- The bedroom loses 1 ft of depth.
- Hanging length does not grow.
It solves 'tight' by giving the rooms a shape, not by adding space.
options.conflicts_with_decisions: Moves the WC away from Melissa's draft-G position (toilet on the left wall). Her 'wall between the vanities' becomes vanities on opposite walls. No island, which honors her note. No wet room. Office, slider, side porch and laundry are unchanged.

options.title: Push the back wall out 7 ft: a 20 x 13'-6" island closet and a 20 x 12 bath (recommended)

Move the primary back wall from y -2.5 to y -9.5: 20'-0" x 7'-0" = 140 sf added. The bedroom stays exactly 20'-0" x 16'-0", and the bath/closet wall moves from y 8 to y 2.5.

CLOSET, 86-106 x 2.5-16 (20'-0" x 13'-6", 270 sf; was 160):
- A 4'-6" dressing spine along the office wall, with a full-length mirror and bench.
- Sliding glass-front wardrobes, 15 ft on both long walls (about 30 LF single-hang, about 45-50 LF with double-hang), all 24" deep.
- A 7'-0" x 2'-0" drawer island with 42" aisles on both sides.
- A shoe tower, and the existing x 106 window becomes a window seat.

BATH, 86-106 x -9.5 to 2.5 (20'-0" x 12'-0", 240 sf; was 210):
- A 5'-6" freestanding tub centered on the back wall under a 7 ft tempered window.
- Her 6 ft vanity on the x 86 wall, with a high clerestory above the mirror because the terrace is outside that wall.
- His 6'-6" vanity on the closet wall; about 6'-7" of open floor between his vanity and the tub.
- Walk-in shower 6'-0" x 7'-0" (about 5'-6" x 6'-7" clear, about 3x today) with a bench and a clerestory.
- Private 6'-0" x 5'-0" WC with a hinged out-swing door (4 ft clear in front of the bowl).
- Linen tower beside the shower.

BEDROOM AND LAUNDRY: unchanged.
options.roof_impact: Low. Change Roof('Primary bath', 86, -2.5, 106, 20) to y1 = -9.5. The same 20 ft hip and the same ridge (about 17'-8"), which stays coplanar with the main office/primary roof, so there are no new valleys. Also update PLATES (86, -9.5, 106, 40) and the SHELL points (86, -9.5) and (106, -9.5). Add a gutter on the back eave.
options.tradeoffs:
Pros: it fixes the closet (Michael's main complaint) and makes a real luxury bath, for the simplest possible roof change.

Cons:
- 140 sf of slab, wall and roof.
- On the current long-pond drawing, the new corner (86, -9.5) is only about 3.8 ft from the water, and about 2.4 ft at the eave. The pond is being reshaped anyway: hold at least 5 ft from the coping, or stop at y -8.5 (120 sf, an 11 ft bath, a 6x6 shower).
- The bath is still reached through the closet's dressing spine (a short, clean path).
- The tub window looks back toward the waterfall bank and garden; the pond itself lies to the back-left.
- The tub, shower and x 86 windows need tempered glass.
options.conflicts_with_decisions: The closet island contradicts Melissa's draft-G 'no closet island'. Her yes is needed, or swap it for a 7 ft bench or ottoman. The WC moves to the back-right, away from her left-wall toilet. Her 'wall between the vanities' is honored by putting the vanities on different walls. No wet room. Office sound walls, slider, side porch and laundry are untouched.

options.title: Full luxury: widen to x 112 for his and her closets and a 26 ft bath
options.problem: Even after B, the couple shares one closet and the bath is 20 ft wide. The ground behind the side porch (x 106-112, y < 16) is unused.
options.proposal:
Grow the back block to x 86-112 by y -9.5 to 16: 293 sf added, about 1,070 sf suite including walls. The bedroom (shifted 1 ft left), slider and laundry stay.

VESTIBULE AND MORNING BAR, 86-91 x 2.5-16 (5'-0" x 13'-6"):
- Coffee counter and undercounter fridge on the office wall, with no sink so the sound wall is not penetrated.

HER CLOSET, 91-103 x 2.5-16 (12'-0" x 13'-6", 162 sf):
- 24" wardrobes on both long walls.
- A 5'-0" x 2'-0" island with 42" aisles.

HIS CLOSET, 103-112 x 2.5-16 (9'-0" x 13'-6", 122 sf):
- 4'-6" aisle and a window seat.
- Its own 2'-4" door from the bedroom at x 103.2-105.6 (the bed and nightstands shift 1 ft left), plus a link to her closet and a hinged door to the bath.

BATH, 86-112 x -9.5 to 2.5 (26'-0" x 12'-0", 312 sf):
- A 5'-6" freestanding tub centered under a back window.
- Her 6 ft vanity on the x 86 wall with a clerestory; his 7 ft vanity on the closet wall.
- Makeup/linen tower and a chaise.
- Walk-in shower 8'-0" x 6'-0" (about 7'-6" x 5'-6" clear) with windows on two walls.
- Private 5'-0" x 6'-0" WC with a pocket door and a window.
options.roof_impact:
Medium.
- Lengthen the 'Primary bath' hip over x 86-106 to y -9.5, as in B, so it stays coplanar with no valleys.
- Cover the x 106-112 strip by extending the side-porch standing-seam shed back to y -9.5 (3:12, high side at x 106, about 10'-4"), tucked under a trimmed bath-hip eave.
- A 26 ft cross-hip was rejected because it makes a dead-level valley at x 96.
- The ceilings in his closet, the shower and the WC slope from about 10'-4" to about 8'-11" (or go flat at 8'-6").
- Re-run roofkit.
options.tradeoffs:
The true luxury suite: separate closets, a 312 sf bath, light on three sides. But:
- Almost 2x the cost of B, and the most roof work.
- The side porch loses its open back end and its post at (111.5, 16.5), becoming an inset porch between the new wing and the garage.
- The dressing-room window at x 106 and the WC window become interior.
- The ceilings in his half slope lower.
- The same pond and terrace setback and tempered-glass notes as B.
options.conflicts_with_decisions: Her closet island versus Melissa's no-island note (a bench is the alternative). The WC moves to the far right. It changes the side porch's back end; porch screening is still open for discussion. No wet room. The office and its sound walls, the slider and the laundry are kept.

primary.why:
B fixes exactly what Michael called tight.
- The closet goes from a 160 sf corridor with a 3'-7" aisle to a 270 sf room with 42" aisles, an island, 24" hanging and a window seat.
- The bath becomes a 240 sf zoned room: a freestanding tub, a shower about 3x today's size, a private WC and split vanities.
- It adds 140 sf with the simplest roof change in the set: the hip end slides back, with the same ridge and no new valleys.
- The bedroom, office, slider and laundry are untouched.
A is the fallback if no footprint can be added, but it does not add storage. C is the step up if budget allows, at about 2x the added area and with more roof and side-porch changes. Before setting B's back wall, confirm the reshaped pond keeps at least 5 ft from the new corner.

great.current:
Living: 24-52 x 34-62.5, 28'-0" x 28'-6" (798 sf), flat 12'-0" beamed ceiling.
Kitchen: 52-68 x 34-59, 16'-0" x 25'-0" (400 sf), flat 11'-0". The courtyard notch (52-68 x 59-62.5) sits in front of it.

- The arrival axis (x 37.5, front doors to the 16 ft glass wall) is blocked by chairs, the coffee table and a 10'-6" sofa that has its back to the pond.

options.title: Plan re-set and notch fill, flat ceilings kept
options.problem: The arrival axis is blocked on foot, nothing lines up across the room, the kitchen front is notched, and the 1 ft ceiling step at x 52 looks like a mistake.
options.proposal:
CROSS AXIS AT y 48.25 (under the ridge):
- The range moves 1'-8" forward to center on y 48.25, still on the stair wall directly behind the island, under the plaster hood.
- The island becomes 13'-6" x 5'-11", centered on the axis (55.5-61.4 x 41.5-55.0), with 49" to the range and 5 stools.
- The media wall is re-centered on y 48.25 (y 41.25-55.25), with the TV on center.
- A chandelier hangs at (37.5, 48.25), where the two axes cross.

ENTRY GALLERY: x 34.5-40.5 is kept clear from the front doors to the glass wall, a 6'-0" x 28'-6" walk. The furniture splits into two rooms either side:
- TV group: a 10 ft sofa with its back to the gallery, about 7 ft from the screen.
- View group: a 6 ft settee and two lounge chairs facing the glass wall and the pond.

FILL THE COURTYARD NOTCH: the kitchen front wall moves from y 59 to y 62.5. The kitchen becomes 16'-0" x 28'-6" (456 sf), and the sink run moves to the front wall under a new 10'-0" window centered on the sink. The front ecosystem pond moves forward to y 63.5-71.5, where the sink window looks straight at it.

FRONT LIVING WINDOWS: from 6'-0" to 7'-0", still centered on the glass-wall edges, with engineered portal framing.

x 52 STEP: becomes a deliberate cypress-wrapped beam with its soffit at 11'-0".
options.roof_impact: None to the planes. Filling the notch removes the 16 ft courtyard eave beam and a re-entrant corner, so the front eave runs straight from x 24 to 78.5. The wider front windows need portal frames under the front porch shed.
options.tradeoffs:
Low cost, and it changes the arrival more than anything else here. But:
- It does not change the volume: the room is still 12 ft and 11 ft flat.
- The range shift moves its gas line and hood duct (still only on paper).
- The media wall shortens from 15'-8" to 14'-0", and the drawn console and entry tree are dropped or moved behind the TV-group sofa.

options.conflicts_with_decisions: None broken. The range stays behind the island on the stair wall, the island keeps its 6 ft width and 48"+ aisle, and the glass wall, no foyer, no entry band and no living fireplace are all kept. It moves the front water feature from Melissa's sketch forward about 3 ft, and changes the hand-drawn furniture, which Michael is now inviting.
options.ceiling: Living flat 12'-0" with cypress beams about every 4 ft running to the front doors (unchanged). Kitchen flat 11'-0" (unchanged). Cypress beam at x 52, soffit 11'-0".

fixtures.label: Sink run on new front wall

options.title: G1 plus a true cathedral living room: ridge beam, cypress timber trusses on the axis lines, portal at x 52 (recommended)
options.problem: A 12 ft flat ceiling over a 28 ft square room reads as wide, not grand (ratio 0.42). About 9 ft of height already sits unused in the roof.
options.proposal:
Everything in G1, plus a cathedral over the living room.

STRUCTURE:
- Frame x 24-52 with 8:12 rafters from the 12'-0" plates up to a structural glulam ridge beam on y 48.25 (engineer to size it; about 5-1/8" x 21" to 6-3/4" x 24").
- The ceiling rises from 12'-0" at the walls to about 20'-6". The beam soffit is about 19'-0".
- Three sinker-cypress collar-tie trusses at x 29.5, 37.5 and 45.5, with ties at about 15'-6". The outer two line up with the glass-wall jambs and porch posts; the middle one sits on the front-door axis.
- Decorative sloped cypress rafter beams between them at x 25.5, 33.5, 41.5 and 49.5, so Michael's beams still come every 4 ft and still run to the front doors.
- The ridge beam's left end bears on a post inside a thickened x 24 wall, with a footing and hold-down.

PORTAL AT x 52: a timber girder truss with its bottom chord at 11'-0", which matches the flat kitchen ceiling, so the step becomes a deliberate portal. The infill above it closes off the kitchen attic.

x 24 END WALL: becomes a symmetric 20 ft focal wall. The media built-in goes up to about 9-10 ft, with cypress paneling above.

Kitchen, scullery and dining stay flat. The stairwell stays open to the roof slope.
options.roof_impact: None outside: the same gable, plate and ridge. Inside, the trusses over x 24-52 become rafters plus a ridge beam, with posts down to footings at (24, 48.25), (52, 34) and (52, 62.5); the last two already carry the dining beam and the front wall. Spray foam goes between the rafters, which the conditioned-attic spec already calls for. HVAC becomes two zones (the bedroom-wing attic and the kitchen/scullery attic), with low returns.
options.tradeoffs:
The biggest jump in grandeur for zero added roof (rough, unverified estimate +$45-80k over G1). But:
- Ducts can no longer cross the living room, so plan two air handlers, which is likely needed at this size anyway.
- The room sounds livelier: use rugs and an acoustic plaster panel.
- Fans and lights need a lift for service.
- The top of the vault gets no direct light (G3 adds it).
- The front doors are capped at 9'-0" unless the front porch shed tie is raised.
- The back-wall steel portal or moment frame at the glass wall is likely needed in ANY scheme, because so little solid wall is left on y 34.
options.conflicts_with_decisions: This explicitly revisits Michael's 12 ft flat beamed living ceiling. The beams are kept every 4 ft and still run to the front doors, so 'no entry band' holds. Kitchen 11 ft, the plaster hood, no living fireplace, the 16 ft glass wall and HVAC in the conditioned attic are all kept. It inherits G1's front-pond move.
options.ceiling: Living: cathedral, 12'-0" at y 34 and y 62.5, rising 8:12 to about 20'-6" at y 48.25. Ridge beam soffit about 19'-0". Cypress collar ties at about 15'-6" (x 29.5, 37.5, 45.5). Kitchen: flat 11'-0", matching the x 52 portal chord. Dining: 11'-6" under its shed. Scullery flat. Stairwell open to the roof slope. Glass wall 10'-0". Front doors 9'-0".

Ridge post in thickened x 24 wall
Sink run on new front wall

options.title: G2 plus a pond-facing gable dormer with clerestory glass on the axis
options.problem: Even with a cathedral, all of the living room's daylight comes in below about 10 ft. The porch roofs tie in at 11'-6" (back) and 10'-11" (front), so neither long wall can take transoms, and the top of a 20 ft vault would be the darkest part of the room.
options.proposal:
Build G2, then add a 16'-0" wide gable dormer on the back slope, centered on the axis over the glass wall (x 29.5-45.5).
- Same 8:12 pitch, on 14'-6" cheek walls (y 34-37.75).
- Its ridge (about 19'-10") dies into the main slope at y about 45.75, in front of the ridge beam.
- Glazing: a 15 ft x 2 ft band from 12'-6" to 14'-6" plus the 16 ft x 5'-4" triangle above, about 55-60 sf net, in bronze or steel mullions to match the glass wall.
- Impact-rated, low-SHGC glass with motorized shades.
- The collar-tie trusses at x 29.5 and 45.5 frame the dormer opening exactly.
From the front doors the view rises: doors, glass wall and pond, then sky above the porch roof.
options.roof_impact: Adds one back-facing 8:12 gable dormer and two valleys to the main back slope. Both valleys drain onto the back porch shed, so they need diverters or crickets and an oversized porch gutter. The steel header or moment frame with wind girts carries the gable wall over the 16 ft glass opening. It is not visible from the street. Re-run roofkit.
options.tradeoffs: The most dramatic room in the house, and the back elevation's feature. But it costs about +$40-70k over G2 (rough, unverified). It adds the valley and flashing risk that the draft L cleanup removed. The heat gain is unknown until north is known. It needs more steel at the glass wall.
options.conflicts_with_decisions: Touches 'hip roofs on the wings, one main gable': it adds a subordinate rear dormer, so Michael must approve it. All G2 notes apply (it revisits the 12 ft flat ceiling).
options.ceiling: Living: cathedral 12'-0" to about 20'-6" (as G2). Dormer vault x 29.5-45.5 from y 34 to about y 45.75: cheek walls 14'-6", peak about 18'-6" inside. Clerestory sill 12'-6", top at the apex. Kitchen flat 11'-0".

great.why:
G2 answers 'big, open, grand' directly.
- The living room goes from a 12 ft flat ceiling to a roughly 20'-6" cathedral inside the roof the house already has, with no new roof form.
- G1's plan moves come with it: a clear 6 ft entry gallery to the glass, a cross axis tying the TV, chandelier, island and range on y 48.25, the courtyard notch filled so the kitchen gets 3'-6" deeper with a real front window, and furniture that faces the pond.

proposals.assessment:
MEASURED CURRENT STATE (draft L). The bath and dressing-room fixtures in plan-generator.py are drawn inside translate(0,-2.5); every y value below has that shift applied. Inches are written with two apostrophes ('').

Primary wing: x 86-106 (20'-0'' wide) by y -2.5 to 32 (34'-6''), 690 sf. The laundry, 91-106 x 32-40 (15'-0'' x 8'-0'', 120 sf), sits in front of it. The only exterior walls are the back wall (y -2.5), the side wall (x 106) and a 7'-6'' stub of the x 86 wall behind the office (y -2.5 to 5). The rest of x 86 is the office's sound wall.

1) PRIMARY BATH, 86-106 x -2.5 to 8 (20'-0'' x 10'-6'', 210 sf). The area is fine by luxury standards. The shape is the problem: it is a 10'-6'' strip with everything in a line.
- WC: 86-91.8 x -2.5 to 2.5 (5'-10'' x 5'-0''). Toilet on the left wall; 2'-5'' door at x 89.2.
- Tub: a 6'-2'' x 3'-0'' drop-in at 92.2-98.4 x -2.1 to 0.9, wedged into the 8'-2'' slot between the WC wall (x 91.8) and the shower wall (x 100). It cannot read as a freestanding tub.
- Shower: 6'-0'' x 5'-0'' nominal (about 5'-7'' x 4'-7'' clear).
- Vanities, along the dressing-room wall: an 8'-10'' double (90.8-99.6), a fin wall, her lone 2'-7'' single (100-102.6) and a tower (104.1-105.6). That is three sinks, unevenly split.
- Sink-to-wall clearance: from the vanity fronts (y 6.1) to the WC/shower walls (y 2.5) is 3'-7''. The ottoman (y 3.0-4.1) cuts that to about 2'-0'', so two people at the sinks back straight into the tub/WC zone.
- Entry: the 2'-10'' bath door (x 87, y 8) opens into a 5'-10'' x 5'-6'' corner that also holds the WC door and the linen opening. The first thing you see is the toilet-room door.

2) DRESSING ROOM, 86-106 x 8-16 (20'-0'' x 8'-0'', 160 sf gross). It is really a corridor with closets.
- The 4'-7'' strip at x 86-90.6 (37 sf) is just the route from the bedroom opening (87-90 at y 16) to the bath door. Only about 109 sf actually stores clothes.
- Wardrobes: two runs of 13'-7'' at 2'-0'' (90.6-104.2 x 8.2-10.2 and 14-16), about 27 LF of rod in total. The last review noted they are drawn about 19'' deep, and hanging clothes need 24''. A couple in a house at this level typically has 50-70 LF.
- Aisle: 3'-10'' nominal, about 3'-7'' clear. Opening the hinged glass fronts (20-24'') leaves about 1'-7''.
- One 3'-0'' end window, and the full-length mirror is drawn over it.
That is why it feels tight: an 8'-0'' depth cannot hold 24'' hanging on both sides plus a comfortable 42'' aisle, let alone an island.

3) BEDROOM, 86-106 x 16-32 (20'-0'' x 16'-0'', 320 sf). Generous. Bed 94.1-101.9 on the closet wall, 8'-0'' slider at x 106 (y 20-28), TV on the y 32 wall. It can give up a foot or two without hurting.

4) LAUNDRY. A good size; it shares the sound wall with the bedroom. It does not connect to the closet; a closet-to-laundry link is a common luxury feature.

DIAGNOSIS. Bath, closet and bedroom are three full-width strips stacked front to back, with all circulation squeezed along the x 86 side. More square footage alone will not fix that; the strips need to become rooms. To give each room a real shape you have to either:
- split the back zone side by side (option P1, zero growth), or
- add depth or width (P2 pushes the back wall out 7'-6''; P3 adds a 7'-0'' bay on the right that lines up with the garage side wall at x 113).

Benchmarks used:
- Bath: 200-260 sf; split vanities of 60''+ each; private WC; freestanding tub with 6''+ clear around it; shower 36''x36'' minimum, 60''x72'' preferred.
- Closet: 150-250 sf, 24'' hanging, 36-42'' aisles, island where the width allows (24''+2x36''+2x24'' = 12'-0'' clear minimum), natural light.
- IRC: WC 30'' wide and 21'' clear in front of the bowl; shower 30''x30'' and 900 sq in minimum; tempered glass at tub and shower windows.

Earlier decisions these options touch:
- Melissa's draft-G markup said NO closet island, a WC toilet on the left wall with shelves open to the bath, and a wall between the vanities. P1 has no island. P2 and P3 add one and need her yes.
- No wet room: all three keep tub and shower separate.
- Office, slider, side porch, laundry and garage are untouched.

Recommendation: P2. It gives the biggest gain for the simplest roof change (the hip end just moves back, the ridge is unchanged).

I checked P1 against plan-generator.py (ROOMS lines 44-47, PARTS, WINDOWS, DOORS and the fixtures drawn inside translate(0,-2.5) at lines 366-374). Nothing overlaps the shell, office, laundry or side porch. The defects:
(1) Rod length is overstated. The two drawn runs (y 0-15.5 and y 0-11.8) total 27.3 LF. Today's two 13'-7'' runs are 27.2 LF. So P1 adds no hanging length at all, not '30-33 LF'. The gain is only the 5'-7'' aisle, the window and the room shape.

proposals.assessment:
CURRENT PRIMARY SUITE (draft L, from plan-generator.py): bedroom 86-106 x 16-32 (20 ft x 16 ft, 320 sf), dressing room 86-106 x 8-16 (20 x 8, 160 sf), bath 86-106 x -2.5-8 (20 x 10 ft 6 in, 210 sf). The suite totals about 690 sf. Comparable luxury primaries run 900-1,200 sf.

Why it feels tight:
(1) Dressing room. The bedroom opening (x 87-90 at y 16) and the bath door (x 87 at y 8) turn the left 4 ft 7 in (x 86-90.6) into a corridor. What's left is a 13 ft 7 in run with 2 ft wardrobes on both sides (y 8.2-10.2 and 14.0-16.0) and a 3 ft 9 in aisle between them. It's a walk-through corridor closet with about 27 lf of rod (about 40 lf if double-hung), no island, no place to stand and dress, and one 3 ft window.
(2) Bath. All three wet fixtures sit in one 5 ft band along the back wall:
- WC 5 ft 10 in x 5 ft at x 86-91.8.
- Drop-in tub 6 ft 2 in x 3 ft under the only real window (x 92-98).
- Shower about 5 ft 5 in x 4 ft 2 in clear (about 23 sf) at x 100-106. That meets the IRC minimum of 30 x 30 in and 900 sq in, but it's far from a luxury 5 x 8.
- The 8 ft 10 in double vanity (x 90.8-99.6) faces the back of the tub across 5 ft 2 in of floor, and you reach the bath only by walking through the closet.
(3) No pond view anywhere in the suite. The pond's right lobe and lily cove are at x 72-85, y -6 to -28, just back-left of the suite. The office (x 68-86) and the terrace (TERR_L turns at (86, -5.6)) take the whole pond frontage. The x = 86 wall of the bath, the only wall that looks straight down the 76 ft length of the pond, has no window. The bedroom looks only at the side porch.

ROOM TO GROW:
- Back (smaller y): about 7 ft. At y -9.5 the corner (86, -9.5) is about 5-6 ft from the shore near (80-82, -9 to -11). Past y -10 the house crowds the lily cove and the pond's liner and coping. Treat y -9.5 as the practical limit, and have the pond builder confirm the setback for the footing.
- Right (x > 106): only for y < 16. The side porch (106-112, y 16-40) and the laundry door (y 32.3) stay as they are.

ROOF: the suite already has its own hip, Roof('Primary bath', 86, -2.5, 106, 20), plate 11, 8:12, ridge about 17 ft 8 in, tucked under the office/primary hip (ridge about 23 ft 8 in at x 87).
- Pushing back within x 86-106 just lengthens that hip. In code: Roof y1 to -9.5, PLATES entry (86, -2.5, ...) to -9.5, SHELL points (86, -2.5) and (106, -2.5) to -9.5. Low roof risk.
- Widening to x 112 makes it a 26 ft cross-hip (ridge about 19 ft 8 in). That's still below the main ridge, but it adds two valleys, and the side porch shed then dies into a sidewall.

No decision blocks these options: there's no primary wet room in any of them, the tub and shower stay separate, and the office walls stay sound-isolated.

RECOMMENDATION: P1 is the best value. It's 140 sf, uses the same roof form, and gives a 280 sf dressing room with an island plus a 240 sf bath with a pond-view tub. P2 is the full luxury version (+293 sf). P3 is the bold alternative that gives the pond view to the bedroom instead of the tub.

What you give up:

reviews.problems:
Checked against plan-generator.py (ROOMS lines 44-46, PARTS, WINDOWS, DOORS, OPENINGS, ROOFS line 141, PLATES) and the TERR_L and pond geometry in long.py. I recomputed the pond shoreline with geo.catmull from LQ.

WHAT CHECKS OUT:
- Footprint is 20 x 7 = 140 sf.
- Dressing room is 86-106 x 2.5-16, 20 x 13'-6" = 270 sf. The assessment's "280 sf" is wrong; the proposal's own 270 is right.
- Bath gross is 20 x 12 = 240 sf. Net of the WC (30) and the shower (42), the open bath is 168 sf.
- Aisles either side of the 2'-7" island are 38" (4.75 to 7.95 and 10.55 to 13.75).
- Roof claim is CORRECT. Today the Primary bath hip's right plane is coplanar with the main Office-and-primary right plane: both are 11 + (106-x)*8/12, and the bath ridge at x 96 sits exactly on the main roof plane at 17.67 ft. Lengthening it to y1 -9.5 keeps that, with the same ridge height, no new valleys and no level trough.
- WC passes IRC R307: toilet centerline y 0 gives 30" to each side wall, and there are 4 ft clear in front.
- Shower is about 5'-6" x 6'-7" clear, well over the 30x30 and 900 sq in minimum.
- Bath door at x 87-89.83 / y 2.5 swinging in clears the tub (top at y -2) by about 1'-8".

PROBLEMS:
1. POND SETBACK IS OVERSTATED. The shoreline (LSW) passes (83.1, -11.9). That is 3.8 ft from the new corner (86, -9.5), not "5-6 ft". With a 1 ft roof overhang (ov 1.0), the eave corner at about (85, -10.5) is only about 2.4 ft from the water. That drips onto the pond coping, so it needs a gutter and a footing/liner detail. A 6 ft push (to y -8.5) gives about 4.4 ft.
2. PRIVACY IS UNDERSTATED. TERR_L runs ALONG the x = 86 wall from (86, 5) to (86, -5.6). The tub window's span y -5.6 to -1.5 opens directly onto the main entertaining terrace, not "the end" of it: a guest can stand about 2 ft from the tub. It needs an obscured lower sash or a sill at 54" or more, not just shades.
3. WC POCKET DOOR CANNOT BE BUILT. The x = 100 wall runs only y -2.5 to 2.5 (5 ft). A 2'-6" pocket door at y -1.5 to 1 needs about 5'-3" of straight wall. The pocket can't run past -2.5 (shower glass and wet wall) or past 2.5 (the T at the dressing room wall).
4. THE LINEN TOWER BLOCKS THE WC DOOR. The tower at x 97.75-99.75, y 0.5-2.5 sits in front of 6" of the WC door opening (y -1.5 to 1), leaving about 24" of approach between the tower and the opening.
5. AISLES ARE TOO TIGHT FOR HINGED DOORS. Hinged 24" glass wardrobe doors swinging into a 38" aisle leave about 14" pass-by. Use sliding doors, or narrow the island to get 42" aisles.
6. SAFETY GLAZING. The tub window (x = 86) and the shower clerestory must be tempered per IRC R308.4.5 if within 60" of the tub or shower standing surface. The proposal doesn't mention it.
7. TOILET UNDER A WINDOW. The kept window at (106, -1 to 1.5) lands directly behind the toilet tank. The sill must sit above the tank. That's a minor point.
8. DEMOLITION NOT LISTED. These existing items must be removed:
- PARTS at x 91.8 and x 100 (y -2.5 to 2.5), and (86, 0.9)-(88.2, 2.5).
- OPENINGS (86.2-88, 2.5) and (100.6-103.6, 2.5).
- DOOR (89.2, 2.5).
- DOOR (87, 8), which moves to y 2.5.
- The window at (92-98, -2.5).
- The translate(0 -2.5) furniture block.

NO CONFLICT WITH DECISIONS: no wet room, the tub and shower stay separate, and the office and its sound walls are untouched.
reviews.fixes:
Keep the 7 ft push to y -9.5, but state the setback honestly: about 3.8 ft to the water, about 2.4 ft at the eave. Require a gutter on the back eave, and have the pond builder sign off on the footing beside the coping. FALLBACK: y -8.5 (120 sf) gives about 4.4 ft, with an 11 ft bath and a 6x6 shower.

WC DOOR: replace the pocket with a hinged 2'-6" door at x 100, y -1.75 to 0.75. Hinge it at y -1.75 and swing it out into the bath. The sweep stays 3.5 ft from his vanity corner (97.5, 0.7).

LINEN TOWER: move it to the back wall at x 97.75-99.75, y -9.5 to -7.5. Shorten her vanity to 6'-0" at x 91.5-97.5, and the transom to x 92-97.

ISLAND: make it 2'-0" deep (x 94-101, y 8.25-10.25). That gives 42" aisles. Use sliding or bi-fold glass wardrobe fronts.

TUB WINDOW: tempered glass, with an obscured lower sash or the sill at 54" or more AFF, because the terrace abuts it. Add tempered glass at the shower clerestory.

Roof and SHELL edits are as stated: Roof('Primary bath', 86, -9.5, 106, 20); PLATES (86, -9.5, 106, 40, 11); SHELL (86, -9.5), (106, -9.5).

reviews.problems:
WHAT CHECKS OUT:
- Footprint: back strip 20 x 7 = 140, plus the x 106-112 strip from y -9.5 to 16 (6 x 25.5 = 153) = 293 sf. Correct.
- Room areas: bath 26 x 12 = 312; her closet 12 x 13.5 = 162; his closet 9 x 13.5 = 121.5; vestibule 5 x 13.5 = 67.5. With the 320 sf bedroom that is about 983 sf net, so "about 1,070 with walls" is plausible.
- WC 107-112 x -3.5 to 2.5: toilet centerline 24" from each side wall, 3 ft clear in front. OK.
- Shower is about 7'-6" x 5'-6" clear. OK.
- His closet aisle is 4'-6". OK.

PROBLEMS:
1. ROOF AS DESCRIBED MAKES A LEVEL TROUGH.
- The 26 ft hip with its ridge along y at x 99 (19.67 ft) has a left plane of h = 11 + (x-86)*2/3.
- The main Office-and-primary right plane is h = 11 + (106-x)*2/3.
- These two planes slope toward each other along x and meet in a dead-level valley at x = 96, at about 17'-8", running from about y 5 to y 16. Neither drains along the valley.
- This is the same flat-valley defect at the office/primary that draft L was built to remove (memory: "Flat valley at x 86 (office/primary)"; ROOFS comment: "never in a level trough").
- Running the ridge along x instead makes another level trough at y 10.5 against the main roof's back hip.
- The proposal's "two valleys plus a front hip" doesn't hold up. Reject the roof as written.
2. THE CLOSET-TO-CLOSET OPENING IS BLOCKED. The cased opening at x 103, y 12.5-15.5 runs into her front wardrobes (x 91.25-102.75, y 13.75-15.75), leaving about 15" of usable width.
3. THE POCKET DOOR INTO THE BATH CANNOT BE BUILT. The door at x 103.5-106 on the y 2.5 wall has nowhere for its pocket: to the right it hits the T with the WC wall at x 107; to the left, the T with the closet partition at x 103.
4. THE WC POCKET FITS ONLY JUST. The x 107 wall is 6 ft long, so the WC pocket must slide toward +y and stop short of the y 2.5 corner. Detail it carefully.
5. LOSSES ON THE x 106 WALL: the dressing room window (106, 10.5-13.5) and the WC window (106, -1 to 1.5) are lost. The side porch post (111.5, 16.5) goes, and the porch becomes inset with less light. This is as disclosed.
6. SETBACK AND PRIVACY AT THE TUB: the same as P1. The water is about 3.8 ft away, not 5-6, and the terrace sits against the x = 86 tub window.
7. HIS CLOSET HAS NO OWN DOOR from the bedroom or vestibule. You reach it only through her closet or the bath. That is a real day-to-day nuisance.
8. COFFEE BAR PLUMBING. A coffee bar with an undercounter fridge on the sound-isolated office wall is OK if it has no sink and no supply lines in the double-stud wall. If it gets a sink, that penetrates the sound wall.
reviews.fixes:
ROOF (the key fix):
- Keep Roof('Primary bath', 86, -9.5, 106, 20) as in P1, coplanar and draining.
- Cover the x 106-112 strip by extending the existing side-porch standing-seam shed back to y -9.5: Roof('Side porch', 106, -9.5, 112, 40, kind='shed', hi='x1', H=10.4, pitch=3/12).
- That gives one continuous lean-to plane with no new valleys. It tucks under the bath hip's eave, so trim that eave's overhang over x 106-112 / y < 16, or drop H to about 10.0. Verify in roofkit.
- Interior plate at x 112 is about 8'-11". Ceilings in his closet, the shower and the WC slope from about 10'-4" down to 8'-11", or go flat at 8'-6".
- Roof cost drops from medium to low-medium.

CLOSET OPENING: move the cased opening between the closets to x 103, y 10.75-13.5 (2'-9"), between her island zone and her front wardrobes. Shorten his left wardrobes to y 5-10.5.

HIS CLOSET TO BATH: a hinged 2'-4" door at x 103.6-105.93 on y 2.5, swinging INTO the bath. It sweeps to y 0.17, clear of the WC wall and the makeup tower.

WC: pocket at x 107, y -3.0 to -0.5, sliding toward +y (stops at 2.0).

Tub window: tempered and obscured, plus a back-eave gutter, the same as P1.

reviews.problems:
1. IT SHRINKS THE BATH, which Michael said feels tight.

proposals.assessment:
Where it stands now: the living room is 28'-0" x 28'-6" (x 24-52, y 34-62.5) with a flat 12 ft beamed ceiling. The kitchen is 16'-0" x 25'-0" (x 52-68, y 34-59) with a flat 11 ft ceiling. Both sit under one 8:12 gable that spans 28'-6" front to back (y 34-62.5). The plate is at 12'-0" and the ridge is about 21'-10" at y 48.25. So roughly 9 ft of volume sits in the attic directly above the biggest room in the house.

A 12 ft flat ceiling over a 28 x 28 room gives a height-to-width ratio of about 0.43. That reads as a wide, nice room, not a grand one. Grand great rooms in this price range usually reach 16 to 22 ft at the center, or at least 0.6 to 0.75 of the room width. The roof is already shaped for that, so vaulting costs no footprint and no new roof form. It is the cheapest "grand" the house can buy.

Problems in the current section:
(1) The 11 ft / 12 ft step at x 52 is only 1 ft. With no wall below it, it reads as a soffit or a mistake. It should be either flush or a deliberate portal.
(2) The only daylight is low: the 16 ft glass wall (x 29.5-45.5 at y 34) and the front windows. Neither long wall can take transoms. The back porch roof ties in at 11'-6" and the front porch at 10'-11", against a 12'-0" plate. The living room's two short walls (x 24 and x 52) are interior, and the gable ends are far away at x 7 and x 78.5. So "gable-end transoms" can't light this room. High light needs a raised plate or a back cross gable.
(3) The left wall at x 24 already holds the media built-in (x 24.25-25.8, y 39-54.7, TV at y 46-48.5). It is centered almost exactly under the ridge, so a vault would turn it into a natural 20 ft focal wall.
(4) The kitchen is a poor vault candidate. Its front wall at y 59 is not the eave (the courtyard beam is at y 62.5), so a kitchen vault would be lopsided: 12 ft at the back, about 20 ft at the ridge, about 14'-4" at the front. The plaster hood at x 65, y 44.6-48.5 sits right under the ridge and would have to climb about 19 ft. The attic above the kitchen, scullery and stair hall (x 52-78.5, about 9-10 ft clear under the ridge) is also where the HVAC in the conditioned attic belongs. Keep the kitchen flat and spend the volume on the living room.
(5) Structure: a flat ceiling gives the back wall a ceiling diaphragm. That wall has little solid wall left (the pocket at x 25.1-29.5, glass at 29.5-45.5, the porch door at 47-50). A vault removes that diaphragm, so in a 140-150 mph zone the engineer may want a steel moment frame or a portal at the glass wall. Scissor trusses also spread their bearings by up to about 1 in under load, which a multi-slide glass head and pocket do not tolerate well. A structural ridge beam has no thrust.
(6) The spray-foam conditioned attic makes any vault easy to insulate: the vault is just more conditioned roof deck, with no venting needed. Air reaches the living room through high sidewall grilles in the two interior end walls (x 24 from the bedroom-wing attic, x 52 from the kitchen attic) instead of ceiling registers.
(7) The bonus stair hall (x 68-78.5) and the scullery should stay flat. They hide ducts and the attic access, and the stair's headroom near the ridge is unaffected by any of these options.

Recommendation: change Michael's earlier pick from a 12 ft flat beamed ceiling to a vaulted living room (G2). Keep the cypress beams, but run them up the slopes front to back, still about every 4 ft and still running to the front doors, so the spirit of that decision survives. Keep the kitchen at 11 ft and make x 52 a deliberate timber portal. G1 is the lower-cost version. G3 adds the pond-facing clerestory if they want light high in the room. G4 is the fallback that keeps a flat ceiling. All options are 0 sq ft added. All prices are rough estimates, not quotes.

Kitchen 11 ft, the plaster hood to the ceiling, no living fireplace, the 16 ft glass wall and the HVAC in the attic are all kept. proposals.assessment:
The great room is already big. Living (24-52 x 34-62.5, 28'-0" x 28'-6") and kitchen (52-68 x 34-59, 16'-0" x 25'-0") have no wall between them, so they are one 44'-0" x 28'-6" room of about 1,200 sf, with a 16'-0" x 12'-0" dining alcove behind it. It does not feel grand yet, for four measurable reasons. It does not need more width.

1) Volume. The ceiling is flat at 12' over the living room and 11' over the kitchen, with a 1 ft step at x 52 that cuts the room in two. Above it sits an 8:12 gable with its ridge at about 21'-10" along y 48.25, so roughly 9 ft of volume over the whole 44 ft is hidden in attic. A 12' flat ceiling over a 28'-6" span gives a height-to-width ratio of 0.42, which reads low and wide. Rooms that feel grand usually run 0.6-0.75 (17-21 ft at the peak over a 28 ft span).

2) The arrival axis is open to the eye but blocked on foot, and the seating faces the wrong way. From the front doors (x 34.5-40.5) to the 16 ft glass wall (x 29.5-45.5) the line is about 28 ft, centered on x 37.5. That is right. But you walk into two chairs and a side table at y 52.5, then a coffee table at y 43.6-46.2, then the back of a 10'-6" sofa (x 30.5-41, y 37.2-40.2). That sofa sits 3 ft in front of the glass with its back to the pond view. It faces the front door and sits 90 degrees to the TV on the x 24 wall. With no foyer (decided), the first 8-10 ft inside the door has to be a clear gallery, and nothing marks one now.

3) The kitchen front is broken by the 16'-0" x 3'-6" courtyard notch (52-68 x 59-62.5). It looks odd from the street, it leaves the sink window at x 56-64 looking into a dark 3'-6" recess under the eave, it needs a 16 ft eave beam, and it cuts the kitchen to 25 ft deep. Because of that, the island can only be 10'-2" (y 41.75-51.9). The range (y 45.3-47.8, center 46.55) and the TV (center 47.25) sit near the ridge line (48.25) but not on it, so nothing sets up a cross axis.

4) The dining room is really a breakfast nook. Net of the 2 ft wine wall it is 14'-0" x 12'-0" with a 4'-10" round table for 6. A 44" x 120" table for 10 needs about 3'-6" past each end, so about 17 ft in one direction. Here it fits 8 at most, and only if the wine wall moves. The alcove sits under the 11'-6" shed behind a 16 ft beam, so it reads as a low side room.

Smaller notes:
- The 3'-5" opening to the bedroom wing (x 24, y 34.5-37.9) sits in the corner next to the glass-wall pocket. It cannot grow, because the passage behind it is only 3'-7" deep (34.4-38) and the server room sits at y 38.
- The hall to the office and primary (68-91 x 34-38) opens into the kitchen corner right at the fridge (y 38.2-41.2). That works, but the route from the garage cuts across the dining opening, so keep the island's back end at y 41.5 or later.
- The front living windows (x 26.5-32.5 and 42.5-48.5) are already centered on the glass-wall edges (29.5 and 45.5), which is good. At 6 ft wide they are small for a 28 ft wall.

The options are ranked by value per dollar:
- G2: a cross axis and a furniture and island re-plan. It costs almost nothing and fixes the arrival.
- G1: one vault plus filling the notch. This is the biggest gain in grandeur.
- G3: a real dining room for 10, done by growing the bump-out 5 ft toward the pond.
- G4: a 14 ft plate with a transom band, which goes further than G1.

G2 assumes G1's notch fill so the island can reach 13'-6". Without the fill, the island is capped near 10 ft.

options.title: One vaulted great room: rafter-tie beams at 12 ft, plaster vault to about 19'-6", courtyard notch filled
options.problem: The living room has a flat 12' ceiling and the kitchen a flat 11' one, with a step at x 52, all under an 8:12 gable whose ridge is at about 21'-10" (y 48.25). That is a 0.42 height-to-width ratio over a 28'-6" span, and about 9 ft of volume across 44 ft is lost to attic. The 16'-0" x 3'-6" courtyard notch (52-68 x 59-62.5) breaks the front wall. It also leaves the kitchen 25'-0" deep and the sink window facing a dark recess.
options.proposal:
Vault: open x 24-68, y 34-62.5 to the roof. Rafters are 8:12, 2x12 or LVL, with spray foam under the deck, which the conditioned-attic spec already calls for. The finished ceiling runs from 12'-0" at the front and back walls to about 19'-6" along the ridge at y 48.25. That is a 0.68 ratio over the span.

Beams: Michael's sinker cypress beams stay at 12'-0" and become the rafter ties. There are six 8"-wide timber ties across the full 28'-6" span at x 25.5, 33.5, 41.5, 49.5, 57.5 and 65.5. The 8 ft bay between 33.5 and 41.5 is centered on the door and glass-wall axis (x 37.5), so no beam crosses the axis. A shallow cypress ridge board at y 48.25 runs the full 44 ft. The beams therefore still read at 12 ft, and the plaster or limewashed board ceiling lifts above them.

One ceiling for living and kitchen: this removes the 12'/11' step at x 52.

End walls: the interior walls at x 24 (lounge and bedroom wing) and x 68 (stair and scullery) become the vault's two gable-shaped end walls. They are full-height plaster.

Notch: move the kitchen front wall from y 59 to y 62.5, so the front wall runs straight from x 24 to 78.5. The kitchen goes from 16'-0" x 25'-0" (400 sf) to 16'-0" x 28'-6" (456 sf). The sink run moves to the new wall (52.4-67.8 x 60.25-62.25), under a 10'-0" window (x 55-65) centered on the sink at x 60. The 16 ft courtyard eave beam is deleted.

Dining: the alcove stays under its shed at 11'-6", as a lower alcove off the vault. The 16 ft beam at y 34 becomes its framed opening.
options.roof_impact: No change to the roof planes. The main 8:12 gable already covers x 7-78.5, y 34-62.5. Framing changes from ceiling joists to rafters with raised timber ties plus a ridge board. The ties at the 12 ft plate need an engineer's check for thrust, and a structural ridge beam is an option. Filling the notch removes an eave beam and a re-entrant corner under the front of the main roof, so the eave runs straight from x 24 to 78.5. The attic over the great room goes away, so the HVAC and water heater stay in the conditioned attic over the office and primary hip (x 68-106) or the stair and scullery bay (x 68-78.5). The great room is served by high sidewall supplies in the x 24 and x 68 end walls.
options.tradeoffs:
Pros:
- This is the largest gain in grandeur for the money, and the room's footprint does not change.
- The 12 ft beams Michael picked are kept, only now as ties, with sky above them.
- The kitchen gains 3'-6" of depth and a real front window.

Cons:
- Rafters, ties and taller plaster cost more than flat trusses, and air volume rises about 50%. A two-stage or variable-speed system plus ceiling fans on the tie beams help.
- A hard plaster vault echoes. Use acoustic plaster on the vault faces, big rugs, and upholstered furniture.
- The plaster hood either runs as a tall chimney to about 19 ft (dramatic) or stops at a 12 ft tie, with a plaster shelf.
- Recessed lighting gets hard in a vault, so light comes from the ties, wall sconces and lamps.
- Ducts can't run over this room.
options.conflicts_with_decisions: This revisits the ceiling plan: living 12' beamed, kitchen and dining 11' flat (Michael's picks). The beams stay at 12 ft as ties, so the beamed look and height he chose are kept, and only the ceiling above them lifts. The plaster hood 'to the ceiling' now meets a vault, so he needs to pick a tall chimney or a stop at the tie. HVAC stays in the conditioned attic, just not over this room. The glass wall, the range behind the island, no foyer, no entry band, and no living fireplace are all unchanged.

reviews.problems:
Verified: the notch is 52-68 x 59-62.5, so filling it adds 56 sf (16 x 3.5). The kitchen goes from 400 to 456 sf. The main gable is x 7-78.5, y 34-62.5, plate 12, 8:12, ridge on y 48.25. Rise is 14.25 x 8/12 = 9.5 ft, so the roof top is about 21'-10". An interior peak of about 19'-6" is plausible once rafter or ridge depth comes off. The 0.42 to 0.68 ratios check out. Problems:
(1) STRUCTURE IS UNDERSTATED. Six timber ties at 8 ft o.c. are not prescriptive rafter ties. IRC R802.4.6 / R802.5.2 want ties at no more than 4 ft o.c. in the lower third, with heel-joint nailing per table. At 8 ft this becomes an engineered heavy-timber truss and purlin system or a structural ridge. A ridge beam spanning 44 ft clear (x 24-68) at about 1,000 plf is not practical without posts. Two of the ties (x 33.5, 41.5) land on the 16 ft glass-wall header at y 34, which already spans a 20.4 ft opening including the pocket. A 28'-6" one-piece sinker cypress tie is a very expensive length, so expect boxed or spliced ties. 'Engineer's check' and cost 'medium' understate this. Call it medium-high.
(2) It breaks Michael's pick. The ceiling table says beams 'about every 4 ft'. G1 halves that to 8 ft (11 beams down to 6) without saying so.
(3) HOOD COLLISION. The tie at x 65.17-65.83 runs straight through the plaster hood footprint (x 65.0-67.8). The 'tall chimney' option can't be built as drawn.
(4) DINING SHED KINK, NOT MENTIONED. The dining shed (Roof 'Dining' y 22-42, 11.85 at y 22, 2:12) is 13.85 at y 34, above the great room's 12 ft plate. It meets the 8:12 plane at y ≈ 37.7, about 14.5 ft up. So in a vault, the strip of kitchen ceiling at x 52-68, y 34-37.7 sits under the low-slope shed, not the vault. That needs a section and a decision: accept a 2:12 soffit strip, or re-detail.
(5) It conflicts with the FRONT WATER FEATURE. The courtyard ecosystem pond (decision: 'water feature by the front porch', from Melissa's sketch) is drawn at x 53-67.6, y 60.3-71.6, starting inside the area the fill takes.
(6) HVAC. Putting the air handler 'over the office' undercuts the office's sound isolation (all four walls are sound walls). Over the primary bedroom is also a noise source. The x 68 end wall has the open hall mouth (y 34-38) and the scullery opening (y 53.5-56.8), so it is not a solid wall for supply registers. Long throws (about 22 ft from each end) need Manual J/D. Unverified.
(7) The volume increase is about +41%, not 50%. Flat: 28x28.5x12 + 16x25x11 ≈ 13,976 cf. Vault: 44x28.5 x about 15.75 average ≈ 19,750 cf.
(8) The x 24 and x 68 gable end walls are about 20 ft tall. They need LSL or balloon framing and lateral bracing. Add this to the cost.
reviews.fixes:
1) Tie spacing: put the ties back at Michael's 4 ft, symmetric about the door axis x 37.5: x 27.5, 31.5, 35.5, 39.5, 43.5, 47.5, 51.5, 55.5, 59.5, 63.5 (10 ties, each 8" wide). The 4 ft bay at 35.5-39.5 frames the axis and the chandelier. The last tie (63.17-63.83) clears the hood face (x 65.0) by about 1'-2". At 4 ft o.c. at the plate, these can be real code rafter ties: 2x12 or LVL rafters, with the tie being a steel flat bar or LVL boxed in cypress, connected per IRC R802.5.2 heel-joint table, and an engineer stamps it. Or use cypress-clad timber trusses at 8 ft with purlins, and say plainly that this costs more and changes Michael's beam rhythm.
2) Plaster hood: run it as a chimney to the vault. No tie crosses it.
3) Show the dining-shed junction in a section. The simplest fix is to finish the y 34-37.7 strip as a flat plaster soffit at about 12'-6" that reads as the dining beam's depth.
4) Move the front pond forward to y ≥ 63.5 (x 53-67.5, y 63.5-71.5). The 10 ft sink window then looks straight at it, which is better.
5) Put the air handler in the conditioned attic over the scullery and stair hall (x 68-78.5, y 50.6-62.5) or over the bedroom-wing hip. Not over the office.
6) Volume: +40%. Cost: medium-high.

proposals.assessment:
Whole-house luxury audit of draft L, outside the primary suite and great room. All dimensions are taken from plan-generator.py.

What already works at a high level: the 6 ft pair of front doors sits on a true axis with the 16 ft glass wall (x 29.5-45.5) and the pond. The office is sound-isolated. The scullery has a rated pass door from the garage. There is a 6'-9" x 12'-6" walk-in under the stair. The 4 ft gallery hall (68-91 x 34-38) is fine. Bedroom 3 has a real walk-in (Closet 15.7-24 x 46.7-54, 8'-4" x 7'-4") and an en-suite through a 4 ft vestibule. The primary suite has its own side porch.

Highest-value gaps, ranked:

(1) Garage arrival and primary privacy. The garage-to-hall door (x 87-90 on y 40) lines up exactly with the primary bedroom door (x 87-90 on y 32), 8 ft apart, so coming in from the garage you look straight into the primary bedroom. Coats, shoes and dog gear all land in the main hall, because the drop zone is a 7'-7" x 18" bench in that hall (78.7-86.3 x 38.3-39.8). The 15' x 8' laundry (120 sq ft) shares the garage wall at y 40 (x 91-102.4) but has no door to the garage. A mud-laundry fixes all three problems at no footprint cost (W1).

(2) The guest suites are out of proportion. Bedroom 2 is 24'-0" x 13'-10" (331 sq ft), larger than the 20' x 16' primary bedroom (320 sq ft). Its walk-in closet is only 6'-5" x 4'-2" (27 sq ft), and it has one 9 ft window on a 24 ft room. Bath 2 (13' x 7'-7", 99 sq ft) has a single sink and an open toilet. The bedroom-wing hall is 3'-5" clear, windowless and dark, and the opening from the living room is 3'-5". Luxury targets are 42-48" halls, a 50+ sq ft walk-in per guest room, a 60"+ vanity and a private WC. W2 is offered as input for Melissa's redraw, not as a replacement for it.

(3) The powder room is reached through the office's 4' x 6' vestibule (68-72 x 28-34). Guests walk past Michael's office door, and the office loses what could be a sound lock. Moving the powder door onto the hall wall at y 34 fixes both (W3).

(4) The bonus room stair is code-minimum: run 1 is about 38" wide (x 68.4-71.6), treads are 10", and the 20 risers are 7.6" each (the limit is 7.75"). It works, but it reads as a service stair. Shifting the closet partition from x 71.75 to x 72.25 gives a 42" clear run 1 for 6" of closet. A true 7"/11" luxury stair needs about 3 ft more run, which would take the scullery's kitchen opening, so I don't recommend it unless the stair is redrawn anyway.

(5) Natural light in the circulation. The 68-91 gallery hall, the stair hall and the bedroom hall have no daylight. Solar tubes or a 2' x 4' skylight work through the conditioned attic: one at about (15, 33) in the bedroom hall and one at about (82, 36) in the gallery. This is low cost.

(6) The living-to-bedroom-wing opening is 3'-5". For a 12 ft beamed great room, a 4'-0" cased opening (x 24, y 34.4-38.4, which takes 4" from the passage side) reads as architecture rather than a doorway. Low cost; best handled in Melissa's redraw.

(7) Smaller notes. The front porch is 9'-6" deep (x 24-52, y 62.5-72); 10-12 ft is the luxury norm and would hold real seating either side of the doors. That change is a roof edit on the porch shed only. A screened back porch (still open for discussion) would make the 22' x 14' porch a usable third living room much of the year in Youngsville.

None of these require new roof planes. Two touch standing decisions, and the options say so: W1 changes where the garage door lands, though the drop zone stays left of the door you walk through and the bays and built-ins don't change. W2 sits inside the bedroom wing that Melissa is redrawing.
